question.text: Under the IFSCA Guidelines, what is a 'Shell Financial Institution' in the context of correspondent banking?

answer.text: A financial institution that has no physical presence in the country where it is incorporated and licensed, and is not affiliated with a regulated financial group
A newly incorporated financial institution with less than one year of operations
A financial institution that only deals with shell companies as clients
A subsidiary of a regulated bank operating under a different trade name

explanation.text: The Logic: In standard AML/CFT terminology adopted by the IFSCA Guidelines and FATF, a Shell Financial Institution is a financial institution that has no physical presence in the country in which it is incorporated and licensed and is not affiliated with a regulated financial group that is itself subject to effective consolidated supervision. The lack of meaningful operational presence and supervisory oversight is what makes such entities a high money-laundering / terrorist-financing risk in correspondent banking. The Trap: Age of incorporation, client mix (dealing with shell companies), or operating under a different trade name as a subsidiary of a regulated bank are not the defining features. The defining test is the combination of "no physical presence in the licensing jurisdiction" and "no affiliation to a regulated financial group" — not corporate cosmetics. Note: The cited pages of the NISM-IFSCA-01 workbook (p.80, p.94) confirm that correspondent and business relationships must not be entered into with a Shell Financial Institution, but the precise definition of a Shell Financial Institution as having no physical presence and no affiliation to a regulated financial group was not located in the pages checked. The framing above reflects the FATF / IFSCA general definition.
